name: ADUM7642CRQZ-RL7
title: ADuM7640/ADuM7641/ADuM7642/ADuM7643: 1 kV rms six-channel digital isolators, 20-lead QSOP
summary: A family of six-channel digital isolators built on transformer coupling, in a 20-lead QSOP and rated 1000 V rms for one minute. The four members differ in how many channels run each way, from six forward (ADuM7640) to three each way (ADuM7643); the ADuM7642 has four forward and two reverse. Each side runs from 3.0 V to 5.5 V, so it also translates between 3 V and 5 V logic. Grade A carries data to 1 Mbps and grade C to 25 Mbps, over -40 °C to +105 °C; outputs default high when the input side has no power.
key_figures: 2.2 mA max at 1 Mbps, 11.2 mA max at 25 Mbps (5 V)

notes: Z marks a RoHS-compliant part. Grade A runs to 1 Mbps, grade C to 25 Mbps; the four families differ only in how many channels point each way.

The propagation delay and pulse width distortion columns carry 20/14 ns and 75/50 ns; the 5 V electrical table gives maximum propagation delay 75 ns (A) and 50 ns (C), maximum skew tPSK 20 ns (A) and 14 ns (C), and maximum pulse width distortion 25 ns (A) and 6 ns (C).

operation.text: Six isolated logic channels in one 20-lead QSOP, in four direction mixes: ADuM7640 has all six inputs on side 1; ADuM7641 has five on side 1 and one (E) on side 2; ADuM7642 has four on side 1 and two (D, E) on side 2; ADuM7643 has three each way (C, D, E on side 2). Grade A is rated to 1 Mbps and grade C to 25 Mbps NRZ. Either side runs from 3.0 V to 5.5 V, so the part also shifts levels between 3 V and 5 V logic. The isolation is 1000 V rms, aimed at uses that need functional isolation rather than a 2.5 kV or 5 kV rating.

Each edge at an input goes across the transformer as a short pulse of about 1 ns that sets or resets a bistable decoder on the far side. When an input holds still for more than about 1 µs, refresh pulses carrying its present level keep the output correct at DC. If the decoder sees no pulses for more than about 5 µs it treats the input side as unpowered or failed, and a watchdog forces the output to its default high level. Every channel has its own glitch filter.

With the input side unpowered the outputs sit high; with the output side unpowered they are high impedance. In either case the outputs follow their inputs again within 1.6 µs after the missing supply returns. Input signal edges are to be no slower than 1.0 ms.

The logic pins need no interface parts. Four bypass capacitors of 0.01 µF to 0.1 µF go between pins 1 and 2 (VDD1A), pins 7 and 10 (VDD1B), pins 11 and 14 (VDD2B) and pins 19 and 20 (VDD2A); the lead length from both capacitor ends to the supply pin is to total no more than 20 mm. VDD1A is wired to VDD1B and VDD2A to VDD2B on the board. Where large common-mode transients occur, keep board coupling across the barrier small and make whatever coupling there is reach every pin on one side equally; otherwise the pins on one side can be driven apart past their absolute ratings, with latch-up or damage as the result. With a suitable board the part meets CISPR 22 Class A and Class B (FCC Class A and B) emissions unshielded; AN-1109 covers board layout and stack-up for EMI.

Propagation delay is the time from the input's 50% point to the output's 50% point; tPLH for a rising edge and tPHL for a falling one can differ. Pulse width distortion is the largest difference between the two and shows how well input timing survives the trip. Channel-to-channel matching is the largest delay difference between channels of one part; propagation delay skew is the largest delay difference between separate parts run under the same conditions.

A changing magnetic field induces a voltage in the receiving coil strong enough to flip the decoder the wrong way. The analysis takes 3 V operation, the most sensitive case. Received pulses exceed 1.0 V and the decoder threshold is near 0.5 V, leaving a 0.5 V margin; the allowed flux is the one that induces at most half of that margin. At 1 MHz the limit is 0.5 kgauss, which induces 0.25 V; even at the worst polarity during a pulse, the received pulse drops from over 1.0 V only to 0.75 V. In terms of a nearby current, at 1 MHz a current of 1.2 kA would have to flow 5 mm from the part to upset it. Strong high-frequency fields can also induce error voltages in board trace loops that trip circuits downstream.

Each channel's supply current depends on its supply voltage, its data rate and its output load. Below half the refresh rate a channel draws its quiescent current; above it the current rises linearly with data rate. The totals for VDD1 and VDD2 are the sums over the input and output channels on each side. Per-channel maxima: at 3.3 V, 1.6 mA from 0 Mbps to 1 Mbps and 7.8 mA at 25 Mbps; at 5 V, 2.2 mA from 0 Mbps to 1 Mbps and 11.2 mA at 25 Mbps.

Insulation wears out under long voltage stress, at a rate that depends on the waveform across it. Bipolar AC is the hardest case and sets the 420 V peak working voltage for a 50-year life; unipolar AC (a waveform from 0 V to a limit of either sign that never crosses 0 V) and DC stress the barrier less. A waveform that fits neither the unipolar AC nor the DC case is treated as bipolar AC and held to the 50-year bipolar figure. Accelerated life tests at voltages above the rated working voltage give the acceleration factors used to predict life at working voltage.
